html:
Cuneiform is the earliest known writing system, made of wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay with a reed, invented in southern Mesopotamia around 3200 BCE. The name comes from the Latin cuneus, "wedge".

It began at Uruk as a way to keep accounts: pictures of a sheep, a jar or a sack of grain, with marks for numbers. Over centuries the pictures became abstract groups of wedges, and signs came to stand for sounds as well as things. That let scribes write names, laws, letters and poems.

Cuneiform was first used for the Sumerian language of the Sumerian city-states. It was then adapted for about a dozen other languages:

  • Akkadian, the language of the Akkadian Empire, Babylon and Assyria, which became the language of diplomacy across the Near East.
  • Elamite in Elam, Hittite in the Hittite kingdom, and others.
  • A simplified version for Old Persian.

Hundreds of thousands of clay tablets survive, because clay lasts, and fire bakes it harder. They record trade, law codes such as the Code of Hammurabi, mathematics, astronomy and literature such as the Epic of Gilgamesh.

Alphabets slowly pushed it out, and the last known tablets date to the first century CE. It was deciphered in the nineteenth century, helped by the Behistun Inscription, which repeats the same text in three cuneiform languages, copied by Henry Rawlinson. It is the oldest writing we know, a little older than Egyptian hieroglyphs.
sum: Cuneiform is the earliest known writing system, made of wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay with a reed, invented in southern Mesopotamia around 3200 BCE. The name comes from the Latin cuneus, "wedge".
